description: Cyclic Sort exploits arrays whose values are constrained to a known range (typically 1..n or 0..n-1) by repeatedly swapping each element into its 'correct' index. Once sorted this way in-place, a single pass reveals missing, duplicate, or misplaced values in O(n) time and O(1) space.
important_details: Only applicable when values are bounded within a range tied to the array's length (e.g., 1 to n, or 0 to n-1).
The core loop: while nums[i] is not already at its correct home index, swap it there.
After the sort pass, a second pass checks index i against expected value (i+1 or i) to spot anomalies — missing numbers, duplicates, or misplacements.
Achieves O(n) time and O(1) extra space, beating both sorting (O(n log n)) and hashset approaches (O(n) space) for this class of problems.
other_relevant_details: Recognize this pattern from constraints like 'array contains n numbers from 1 to n' or 'numbers in range [0, n]' — that specific range-tied-to-length signal is the trigger, distinguishing it from generic sorting problems.

variations.variation: Basic Cyclic Sort (Place Every Number at Its Index)
variations.description: Rearrange an array of 1..n (or 0..n-1) so that each value ends up at its natural index, using repeated in-place swaps rather than a comparison sort.
important_details: The while loop (not if) at each index is critical — one swap may bring in a value that also needs to move.
Each element is swapped into place at most once overall, which is what keeps this O(n) despite the nested-looking loop.
Skip the swap if the value is already correctly placed or is a duplicate of the target slot's value (to avoid infinite loops).
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n) amortized (each element moved a bounded number of times). Space: O(1).

variations.description: After cyclic-sorting a 0..n or 1..n range array, scan once to find the single index whose value doesn't match, revealing the missing number.
important_details: Handles the off-by-one boundary carefully depending on whether the range is 0..n (n+1 slots, values 0..n) or 1..n.
If every index matches after sorting, the missing number is the one 'past the end' (n itself).
Alternative O(n) solutions exist via XOR or Gauss sum, but cyclic sort generalizes better to 'find ALL missing' variants.

problems.name: Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array

variations.description: Cyclic-sort the array, then scan for indices where the value doesn't match — those mismatches point directly to duplicate values, without needing extra space.
important_details: Works when there's exactly one duplicate (possibly repeated many times) or multiple duplicates, with a small tweak to how mismatches are collected.
Contrast with the Fast & Slow Pointers 'Find the Duplicate Number' trick — cyclic sort is simpler to reason about but mutates the input array.
If the array cannot be modified, prefer the Floyd's cycle-detection variant instead.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n). Space: O(1). Mutates the input array — call out this trade-off if the problem forbids mutation.

problems.name: Find All Duplicates in an Array

variations.description: The hardest variant: find the smallest missing positive integer in O(n) time and O(1) space by cyclic-sorting only the values that could possibly matter (1..n), ignoring negatives, zero, and out-of-range values.
important_details: Only values in range [1, n] are worth placing — negatives, 0, and values > n are simply skipped during the sort phase.
This is the classic 'Hard'-rated interview question that directly tests mastery of cyclic sort's edge-case handling.
After sorting, the answer is the first index i where nums[i] != i+1, or n+1 if the array is fully 1..n.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n). Space: O(1) — meets the problem's strict constraint that rules out sorting-based or hashset-based solutions.
